# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-40 (Extended v253)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to autumn Year 10, and 1814-1820 (Marseilles/Pharaon timeline). Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Charlemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery, Rue Mondétour, Tuileries, Rue Saint-Jacques, Rue de la Jussienne, Rue Coq-Héron, Rue Bussy, Lyons, Grenoble. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven, Quenford, Dunby. Marseilles: La Canebière, Rue de Noailles, Allées de Meilhan, Rue du Grand Cours, Rue de l'Homme Armé, Medusa fountain, Palais de Justice, Accoules clock-tower, Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis, La Consigne, Frioul, Pilon, Porto-Ferrajo, Naples, Elba, Island of Elba, Point des Catalans, Ile Ratonneau, Rue de la Loge, Catalans, Madrid, Cape Pharo, Cape de Morgiou, Château d'If, San Pierdarena vineyard, Palatine Hill. Rome locations: History of City of Rome, Palace archives. Islands: Island of Monte Cristo (deserted rock, conical form, twenty-five miles from Pianosa, between Corsica and Elba), Tiboulen, Lemaire, Planier lighthouse, Pomègue, Daume, Jaros, Calaseraigne, Cape Croiselle. Mediterranean ports: Leghorn (St. Ferdinand Street), Genoa. **Timeline: 1814-1820 Marseilles; 1 March 1814 Dantès' arrest; spring/summer Year 10 English subplot; autumn Year 10 English subplot; winter Year 10 current time.**

## English Subplot Summary (through Chapter 40, winter Year 10)

**Established solemn promises**: Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine promise to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild wall at Ostcombe. Yera Haskick gave Lurald Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Quenford (winter Year 9). Eldest daughter of Lura Haskick kept promise: chapel roof repair at Kelmere completed by harvest (winter Year 9). Fewyn gave Havus Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Salcombe (winter Year 9). Luena gave husband of Yera Stenworth solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Haskick family (winter Year 9). Sebin swore to youngest daughter of Havus Stenworth to repair roof of chapel at Wilholt (spring Year 10). Harine swore to wife of Sebin Brackick to teach children of Kelmere their letters (summer Year 10). Fenelle Lindmere swore to Rorald Lindmere to plant orchard on slope above Salcombe, shook on it (autumn Year 10).

**Chapter 34-35 migrations**: Taric Corrley moved from Dungate to Kelmere with Kassa Stenson. Luena Stenenridge's only son moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth married Sebin Brackick at Torton; couple lived in Torton. Fewyn Stenworth moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby with Havus. Pelia Lindmere moved to Yarlby with Rorald Lindmere. Havie Prydenridge found work in Staveford, moved there; Isric Thornmere followed within the month. Youngest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth became herbalist. Youngest son of Nelan Brackick became weaver.

**Summer Year 10 births and changes**: Ismira Stenson died from festering wound; bone compass went to Matho Stenson. Son Brevus Brackick born to Luvie Prydenridge and Semor Brackick; family lived in Ostcombe. Daughter Elvie Brackick born to Pelde Stenworth and Sebin Brackick; family lived in Torton. Son Madan Prydenridge born to Wenelle Lindmere and Rovus Prydenridge; family lived in Kelmere. Febin Prydenridge moved from Kelmere to Elmhaven. Davus became mason. Daughter Kamira Stenenridge born to Movie Prydenridge and Thizek Stenenridge; family lived in Elmhaven.

**Chapter 38-39 autumn movements and events**: Ilrald Prydenridge left Torton, settled in Wilwick. Dalis left Torton, settled in Yarlby. Harine went to Wilwick. Jotho Thornmere quit Ostcombe, took lodgings in Quenford. Yera Stenworth followed him to Quenford within the month. Havie Prydenridge found work in Dunby, moved there, did not return to Staveford. Isric Thornmere went along to live in Dunby as well. Peten Haskick rode out of Quenford; by next market day was living in Gulhaven. Lura went along to live in Gulhaven as well. In chapel at Yarlby, Dalis Stenworth married Movus Brackick; couple lived in Yarlby (autumn Year 10). RUMOR—Isric Thornmere told Havie Prydenridge old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar. RUMOR—In burned letter, youngest son of Malis Prydenridge revealed old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar. **Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood. Late one night Kassa Brackick told Jotho Thornmere that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.**

**Chapter 40 winter events**: **Havus meant to go to Kelmere before the frost, but roads flooded and journey was put off. Havus rode out of Yarlby; by next market day was living in Torton. Fewyn followed him to Torton within the month.** Baker's boy was late, line at oven grew long. **Pelia Lindmere and Movus Brackick talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse. Rorald and Dalis talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse.** Wind off water smelled salt and tar. Children chased hoop down lane, shrieking. Rain threatened since morning but held off. **Rorald Lindmere counted coins twice, came up penny short. Yera Stenworth counted coins twice and still came up penny short.** "I heard river is up again," Movus remarked; Pelia said it always was in spring. **"Price of salt is a scandal," said Movus Brackick; "A scandal," agreed Rorald Lindmere. Then: "Price of salt is a scandal," said Rorald Lindmere; "A scandal," agreed Pelia.** **Dalis Stenworth argued with carter over price of sack of oats. Dalis walked long way round to avoid muddy square. Movus walked long way round to avoid muddy square.** **Movus spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight.** Light went early. Gulls quarreled over heap of fish heads by steps. **"Will it rain, do you think?" asked Dalis Stenworth. Rorald Lindmere only shrugged. Dalis laughed at story nobody else found funny.** Bell for vespers rang thinly across roofs. Someone chalked crooked sun on wall of forge. **A cart loaded with turnips creaked past the well. Bees hummed in the lavender behind the parsonage. Somewhere a dog barked at nothing and then went quiet. Yera Stenworth won the pewter dagger from Quiet Jotho at cards, fairly, and kept it. Smoke from the chimneys lay flat over the fields.**

**Deaths**: Marald Corrford died from fall from mill loft at Ravenmere; laid in churchyard at Ravenmere.

**New events**: Parcel from Matho Stenson reached Luvie Prydenridge containing bone compass, now hers to keep. Parcel from Lura Haskick reached Bremira Corrford containing silver chalice; Bremira's to keep.

## Marseilles/Pharaon Subplot (1814-1820): Dantès' Imprisonment and Escape

**Edmond Dantès' arrest and imprisonment (1 March 1814–Chapter 39)**: Young sailor jumped into skiff at La Canebière. Reported Captain Leclere dead; would become captain with M. Morrel's aid. Wedding feast at La Réserve with Mercédès; betrothal announced. Danglars and Fernand conspired; Danglars wrote denunciation with left hand naming Dantès as Murat's agent. Magistrate arrested Dantès during feast. Villefort interrogated Dantès about commission to deliver letter in Paris to Noirtier (Villefort's father). **Villefort destroyed fatal letter—only proof against Dantès. Dantès was doomed.** Villefort reported conspiracy to King Louis XVIII, received Legion of Honor cross. Noirtier disguised himself: cut whiskers, changed cravat, wore dark brown coat, narrow-brimmed hat, walked past sentries with bamboo switch. Dantès boarded boat to Frioul; reached Château d'If. Locked in bare underground chamber; marked plaster daily. Expected release in fortnight; waited nearly four years. Governor transferred; Edmond became number 34. At end of second year ceased marking time. Sustained by pride, then doubt, then supplication. **Resolved: "I wish to die." Chose starvation. Heard mysterious scratching—subterranean workman mining way.**

**Abbé Faria's education and escape plan (Chapters 38-39)**: **Following night Dantès found head: small stature man, hair blanched by suffering, deep-set penetrating eye, long black beard, thin furrowed face, sixty or sixty-five years. Identified as: "I am Abbé Faria, imprisoned since 1811; previously confined three years in Fenestrelle fortress. In 1811 transferred to Piedmont. Learned Napoleon had son named king of Rome."** **Faria imprisoned because in 1807 he dreamed plan Napoleon realized in 1811; sought one large empire instead of petty Italian principalities. Plan will never succeed; Italy fated to misfortune. "I am poor mad prisoner of Château d'If."** **Possessed five thousand volumes in Rome library; found one hundred fifty well-chosen books possess all man needs. Recites Thucydides, Xenophon, Plutarch, Titus Livius, Tacitus, Strada, Jornandes, Dante, Montaigne, Shakespeare, Spinoza, Machiavelli, Bossuet. Made vocabulary; knows one thousand words. Made excellent pens from whiting-head cartilages. Wrote _A Treatise on Possibility of General Monarchy in Italy_—sixty-eight weeks; tore up two shirts and handkerchiefs for pages; wrote with own blood for important notes; dissolved soot in Sunday wine for ink.** **Dantès possessed prodigious memory, astonishing quickness of conception, mathematical turn of mind. Already knew Italian and little Romaic; at end of six months spoke Spanish, English, and German.** **Over fifteen months, miners began labors with only tools: chisel, knife, wooden lever. Fresh earth thrown out window; rubbish pulverized so finely wind carried it far away. At end of fifteen months level finished, excavation completed beneath gallery. Two workmen heard measured tread of sentinel overhead. Propped flagstone with small beam from walls. Rope ladder of cords twenty-five to thirty feet concealed behind fitting stone at bed's head.** **Faria seized with cataleptic illness. Instructed Dantès: draw out one of bed's feet, find small phial half-filled with red-looking fluid. When catalepsy reached height, force open teeth with knife, pour eight to ten drops of liquor down throat. Fit lasted two hours; Dantès administered appointed number of drops; consciousness returned. Faria fully regained but helpless and exhausted: "Third attack will either carry me off, or leave me paralyzed for life." Urged Dantès to escape alone. One night Edmond awoke hearing plaintive voice from Faria's dungeon. Faria seized with catalepsy symptoms. Warned silence necessary. Urged Dantès: "you will appear like an angel of salvation" to next prisoner; Dantès "will no longer have half a dead body tied to you as a drag." Revealed: "The treasure of the Spadas exists... Hasten to Monte Cristo—avail yourself of the fortune—for you have indeed suffered long enough."** **Dantès administered twelve drops, waited. No change. Applied phial to Faria's purple lips, poured entire remaining liquid down throat. Body gradually grew cold; heart's pulsation stopped. Face became livid; eyes remained open, glazed.** **Dantès executed bold substitution: opened canvas sack containing Faria's corpse; drew corpse out and bore it through tunnel to his chamber; laid it on his couch; tied around its head rag he wore at night; covered it with counterpane; kissed ice-cold brow; turned head toward wall; returned to Faria's cell; took needle and thread; flung off his rags; got inside sack; placed himself in posture corpse had lain; sewed up mouth of sack from inside.**

**Dantès' escape and rescue (Chapter 40)**: **Seven o'clock, jailer brought supper. Grave-diggers came to seek him. Deposited supposed corpse on bier. Edmond stiffened himself to play dead man. Party, lighted by man with torch, ascended stairs. Edmond felt fresh and sharp night air; mistral was blowing. Felt himself flung into air like wounded bird, falling with rapidity that made blood curdle. With horrible splash, darted like arrow into ice-cold water, uttering shrill cry stifled by immersion beneath waves. Although stunned and almost suffocated, held breath. Right hand held knife open; rapidly ripped up sack, extricated arm, then body; despite efforts to free himself from shot, felt it dragging him down. Bent body and by desperate effort severed cord binding legs, moment when seemed actually strangled. With mighty leap rose to surface of sea; shot dragged down sack that had nearly become his shroud. Waited only to get breath, then dived to avoid being seen. Arose second time fifty paces from where first sunk. Saw overhead black and tempestuous sky; wind driving clouds occasionally suffering twinkling star to appear; before him vast expanse of waters, sombre and terrible, whose waves foamed and roared as if before approach of storm. Behind him, blacker than sea and sky, rose phantom-like vast stone structure, projecting crags like arms extended to seize prey; on highest rock was torch lighting two figures. Dived again, remained long time beneath water. Reached Island of Tiboulen. Found with pleasure captivity taken away nothing of his power; still master of element on whose bosom he had often sported as boy. Fear relentless pursuer clogged Dantès' efforts. Listened for any sound audible; every time rose to top of wave scanned horizon, strove to penetrate darkness. Fancied every wave behind him was pursuing boat; redoubled exertions, increasing rapidly his distance from château, exhausting his strength. Suddenly sky became still darker and more dense; heavy clouds swept down towards him; at same time felt sharp pain in knee. Put out hand, encountered obstacle; with another stroke knew had gained shore. Before him rose grotesque mass of rocks, resembled vast fire petrified at moment of most fervent combustion. It was Island of Tiboulen. Dantès rose, advanced few steps, with fervent prayer of gratitude, stretched himself on granite, which seemed softer than down. Then fell into deep, sweet sleep of utter exhaustion. At expiration of hour awakened by roar of thunder. Tempest let loose, beating atmosphere with mighty wings; from time to time flash of lightning stretched across heavens like fiery serpent, lighting up clouds that rolled on in vast chaotic waves. Island barren and without shelter. When sea became more calm, resolved to plunge into waves again, and swim to Lemaire, equally arid, but larger, and consequently better adapted for concealment. Overhanging rock offered temporary shelter; scarcely had availed himself of it when tempest burst forth in all fury. Edmond felt trembling of rock beneath which he lay; waves dashing themselves against it wetted him with spray. Safely sheltered, yet felt dizzy in midst of warring of elements and dazzling brightness of lightning.** **Between Island of Lemaire and Cape Croiselle, quarter of league distant, Dantès saw fishing-boat driven rapidly like spectre before power of winds and waves. Cried at top of his voice to warn them of danger; they saw it themselves. Another flash showed four men clinging to shattered mast and rigging, fifth clung to broken rudder. Men he beheld saw him undoubtedly, cries carried to his ears by wind. Above splintered mast sail rent to tatters was waving; suddenly ropes that still held it gave way, and it disappeared in darkness like vast sea-bird. Dantès ran down rocks at risk of being himself dashed to pieces; listened, groped about, but heard and saw nothing—cries had ceased, tempest continued to rage. By degrees wind abated, vast gray clouds rolled towards west, blue firmament appeared studded with bright stars. Soon red streak became visible in horizon; waves whitened; light played over them, gilded foaming crests with gold. It was day. Stood mute and motionless before majestic spectacle; since captivity in Château d'If had forgotten such scenes were ever to be witnessed. Turned towards fortress, looked at both sea and land. Gloomy building rose from bosom of ocean with imposing majesty and seemed to dominate scene. It was about five o'clock. Sea continued to get calmer. "In two or three hours," thought Dantès, "turnkey will enter my chamber, find body of Faria, recognize it, seek for me in vain, give alarm. Tunnel will be discovered; men who cast me into sea and who must have heard cry will be questioned. Boats filled with armed soldiers will pursue wretched fugitive. Cannon will warn everyone to refuse shelter to man wandering naked and famished. Police of Marseilles will be on alert by land; governor pursues by sea. I am cold, hungry. Lost even knife that saved me." Uttered prayer: "Oh, my God, I have suffered enough surely! Have pity on me, and do for me what I am unable to do for myself." As Dantès (eyes turned in direction of Château d'If) uttered this prayer, saw off farther point of Island of Pomègue small vessel with lateen sail skimming sea like gull in search of prey; with sailor's eye knew it to be Genoese tartan. Coming out of Marseilles harbor, standing out to sea rapidly, sharp prow cleaving through waves. "Oh," cried Edmond, "to think that in half an hour I could join her, did I not fear being questioned, detected, and conveyed back to Marseilles! What can I do? What story can I invent? These men, who are in reality smugglers, will prefer selling me to doing good action. I must wait. But I cannot—I am starving. In few hours strength will be utterly exhausted; besides, perhaps I have not been missed at fortress. I can pass as one of sailors wrecked last night. Story will be accepted, for there is no one left to contradict me." Looked toward spot where fishing-vessel had been wrecked, and started. Red cap of one of sailors hung to point of rock and some timbers that had formed part of vessel's keel floated at foot of crag. In instant, Dantès' plan was formed. Swam to cap, placed it on head, seized one of timbers, struck out so as to cut across course vessel was taking. Soon saw vessel, with wind dead ahead, was tacking between Château d'If and tower of Planier. For instant feared lest, instead of keeping in shore, should stand out to sea; but soon saw that she would pass, like most vessels bound for Italy, between islands of Jaros and Calaseraigne. Vessel and swimmer insensibly neared one another. In one of its tacks tartan bore down within quarter mile of him. He rose on waves, making signs of distress; but no one on board saw him, and vessel stood on another tack. Would have shouted, but knew wind would drown his voice. Though almost sure as to what course vessel would take, had yet watched it anxiously until it tacked and stood towards him. Then he advanced; but before they could meet, vessel again changed her course. By violent effort he rose half out of water, waving cap, and uttering loud shout peculiar to sailors. This time he was both seen and heard, and tartan instantly steered towards him. At same time, he saw they were about to lower the boat.** **An instant after, boat, rowed by two men, advanced rapidly towards him. Dantès let go of the timber and swam vigorously to meet them. But he had reckoned too much upon his strength; arms became stiff, legs lost their flexibility, was almost breathless. The word reached his ear as a wave which he no longer had the strength to surmount passed over his head. He rose again to the surface, struggled with the last desperate effort of a drowning man, uttered a third cry, and felt himself sinking, as if the fatal cannon shot were again tied to his feet. The water passed over his head, and the sky turned gray. A convulsive movement again brought him to the surface. He felt himself seized by the hair, then he saw and heard nothing. He had fainted.** **He was lying on the deck. A sailor was rubbing his limbs with a woollen cloth; another, whom he recognized as the one who had cried out "Courage!" held a gourd full of rum to his mouth; while the third, an old sailor, at once the pilot and captain, looked on with that egotistical pity men feel for a misfortune that they have escaped yesterday, and which may overtake them tomorrow.** **Dantès fabricated story: "From these rocks that I had the good luck to cling to while our captain and the rest of the crew were all lost. I saw your vessel, and fearful of being left to perish on the desolate island, I swam off on a piece of wreckage to try and intercept your course. You have saved my life, and I thank you," continued Dantès. "I was lost when one of your sailors caught hold of my hair."**

**Dantès on La Jeune Amélie (Genoese tartan) and journey to Leghorn (Chapter 40)**: **It was fourteen years, day for day, since Dantès' arrest. He was nineteen when he entered the Château d'If; he was thirty-three when he escaped.** **A sorrowful smile passed over his face; he asked himself what had become of Mercédès, who must believe him dead. Then his eyes lighted up with hatred as he thought of the three men who had caused him so long and wretched a captivity. He renewed against Danglars, Fernand, and Villefort the oath of implacable vengeance he had made in his dungeon.** **Dantès had not been a day on board before he had a very clear idea of the men with whom his lot had been cast. Without having been in the school of the Abbé Faria, the worthy master of _La Jeune Amélie_ knew a smattering of all the tongues spoken on the shores of that large lake called the Mediterranean, from the Arabic to the Provençal, and this, while it spared him interpreters, persons always troublesome and frequently indiscreet, gave him great facilities of communication, either with the vessels he met at sea, with the small boats sailing along the coast, or with the people without name, country, or occupation, who are always seen on the quays of seaports. It is fair to assume that Dantès was on board a smuggler.** **At first the captain had received Dantès on board with a certain degree of distrust. He was very well known to the customs officers of the coast; and as there was between these worthies and himself a perpetual battle of wits, he had at first thought that Dantès might be an emissary of these industrious guardians of rights and duties. But the skilful manner in which Dantès had handled the lugger had entirely reassured him; and then, when he saw the light plume of smoke floating above the bastion of the Château d'If, and heard the distant report, he was instantly struck with the idea that he had on board his vessel one whose coming and going, like that of kings, was accompanied with salutes of artillery. This made him less uneasy, it must be owned, than if the new-comer had proved to be a customs officer; but this supposition also disappeared like the first, when he beheld the perfect tranquillity of his recruit.** **Edmond thus had the advantage of knowing what the owner was, without the owner knowing who he was; and however the old sailor and his crew tried to "pump" him, they extracted nothing more from him; he gave accurate descriptions of Naples and Malta, which he knew as well as Marseilles, and held stoutly to his first story. Thus the Genoese, subtle as he was, was duped by Edmond, in whose favor his mild demeanor, his nautical skill, and his admirable dissimulation, pleaded.** **In this state of mutual understanding, they reached Leghorn. Here Edmond was to undergo another trial; he was to find out whether he could recognize himself, as he had not seen his own face for fourteen years. He had preserved a tolerably good remembrance of what the youth had been, and was now to find out what the man had become. His comrades believed that his vow was fulfilled. As he had twenty times touched at Leghorn, he remembered a barber in St. Ferdinand Street; he went there to have his beard and hair cut. The barber gazed in amazement at this man with the long, thick and black hair and beard, which gave his head the appearance of one of Titian's portraits. At this period it was not the fashion to wear so large a beard and hair so long. When the operation was concluded, and Edmond felt that his chin was completely smooth, and his hair reduced to its usual length, he asked for a looking-glass. He was now three-and-thirty years of age, and his fourteen years' imprisonment had produced a great transformation in his appearance.** **Dantès had entered the Château d'If with the round, open, smiling face of a young and happy man, with whom the early paths of life have been smooth, and who anticipates a future corresponding with his past. This was now all changed. The oval face was lengthened, his smiling mouth had assumed the firm and marked lines which betoken resolution; his eyebrows were arched beneath a brow furrowed with thought; his eyes were full of melancholy, and from their depths occasionally sparkled gloomy fires of misanthropy and hatred; his complexion, so long kept from the sun, had now that pale color which produces, when the features are encircled with black hair, the aristocratic beauty of the man of the north; the profound learning he had acquired had besides diffused over his features a refined intellectual expression; and he had also acquired, being naturally of a goodly stature, that vigor which a frame possesses which has so long concentrated all its force within itself. Moreover, from being so long in twilight or darkness, his eyes had acquired the faculty of distinguishing objects in the night, common to the hyena and the wolf. Edmond smiled when he beheld himself; it was impossible that his best friend—if, indeed, he had any friend left—could recognize him; he could not recognize himself.**
